# About this document {.unnumbered}

This document is a reference analysis for the author, not a course page. It shows what
students could do with these data with the tools of Chapters 1 to 7 (RTMB, RTMBdist,
DHARMa and TMB), and follows the structure of the analysis of the infiltration data in
`Case Studies/Infiltration`: the data, an exploration, the model, the choice of curve,
distribution and random effect, the candidates for the change over time, the answer,
checks of the model, a second transect and a simulation of the estimator. Alternatives
are in boxes titled "Alternative" and traps in boxes titled "Pitfall"; @sec-summary lists
them all. `README.md` in this folder describes the sources of the data (the spreadsheet
and the two papers), what is still not known and the suitability of the data for a case
study; `data_description.md` describes the study for students.

::: {.callout-note title="Possible research question (for the author to decide)"}
How did the cline in the frequency of melanic two-spot ladybirds along the east–west
transect change between 1980 and 2004: did the frequency fall inland, rise at the coast,
or did the cline move? The answer below is the typical frequency of melanics at 10 km and
at 60 km from the coast in each survey, and the odds ratio between the two (the height of
the cline), quantities inside the range of every survey.
:::

The document needs RTMB, RTMBdist, DHARMa, TMB and knitr and takes about two minutes to
render, most of it in the simulation of @sec-simulation. The optimisations are
deterministic and every simulation has its own seed. Numbers in the text are calculated
inline from the code, except descriptions of what a figure shows, which were written from
the figures of the run of 20 November 2026 (R 4.6.1).

Status: generated draft (20 November 2026), not reviewed by the author.

# The data {#sec-data}

The two-spot ladybird, *Adalia bipunctata*, has genetically determined colour morphs that
fall into two classes: **melanics**, mostly black with red spots, and **non-melanics**
(*typica*), red with black spots. The melanic alleles are dominant over the non-melanic
one. Under the hypothesis of **thermal melanism**, black beetles warm up faster in sunshine
and have an advantage where it is cool, cloudy and calm (de Jong et al. 1996, cited in
both papers).

Brakefield (1984a) described a steep cline in the frequency of melanics along a transect
from the coast of the south-west Netherlands inland: around 10 to 20% near the coast and
about 55% from about 50 km inland. The transect was sampled again in 1991 and 1995
(de Jong and Brakefield 1998) and in 1998 and 2004 (Brakefield and de Jong 2011). In each
survey, adults and pupae were collected at each locality, mainly on lime trees (*Tilia*),
*Rosa rugosa* and *Euonymus*; pupae were reared in the laboratory, and every beetle was
scored as melanic or non-melanic. The 1980 survey pools collections made between 1978
and 1981 (de Jong and Brakefield 1998). From about 2002 the invasive harlequin ladybird
*Harmonia axyridis* reduced the numbers of *A. bipunctata*, so the 2004 samples are
smaller and five localities could not be sampled (Brakefield and de Jong 2011).

The 1998 paper also resampled a second, north–south transect in 1991 or 1992 (the paper
says 1992, the spreadsheet 1991), whose distances are measured from Delft and not from the
coast. @sec-ns uses it as an extension.

The file `adalia.csv` has one row per sample (a locality in a survey): the transect
(`EW` or `NS`), the locality (`place`), the survey (`year`), the distance (`distance_km`,
to the coast for EW and from Delft for NS) and the numbers of black (melanic) and red
(non-melanic) beetles.

```{r}
adalia = read.csv("adalia.csv")
str(adalia)
```

We analyse the east–west transect first. The localities are ordered from the coast inland,
and each sample gets its size and its proportion of melanics.

```{r}
ew = adalia[adalia$transect == "EW", ]
rownames(ew) = NULL
ew$n = ew$black + ew$red
ew$prop = ew$black / ew$n
ew$site = factor(ew$place, levels = unique(ew$place[order(ew$distance_km)]))
ew$year_f = factor(ew$year)
levels(ew$year_f)

# Colours (Okabe-Ito) and symbols of the five surveys.
year_colours = c("#D55E00", "#E69F00", "#009E73", "#56B4E9", "#0072B2")
year_symbols = c(19, 17, 15, 1, 2)

# Formatting of numbers quoted in the text.
f1 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 1)
f2 = function(x) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = 2)
pct = function(p) formatC(100 * p, format = "f", digits = 0)
big = function(x) format(x, big.mark = ",")
```

# Exploratory data analysis {#sec-eda}

## The design {#sec-design}

The number of beetles in each sample, by locality (rows, from the coast inland) and survey
(columns); a zero means that the locality was not sampled:

```{r}
sample_sizes = xtabs(n ~ site + year, data = ew)
sample_sizes
table(ew$year)
summary(ew$n)
```

There are `r nrow(ew)` samples from `r nlevels(ew$site)` localities between
`r min(ew$distance_km)` and `r max(ew$distance_km)` km from the coast, with
`r big(sum(ew$n))` beetles in all. Only the
`r names(which(colSums(sample_sizes > 0) == nlevels(ew$site)))` survey covers every
locality, and the 2004 survey misses `r nlevels(ew$site) - sum(ew$year == 2004)` of them.
The samples range from `r min(ew$n)` to `r big(max(ew$n))` beetles. The mean sample size per survey shows where the
large ones are:

```{r}
round(tapply(ew$n, ew$year, mean))
```

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the 1980 survey is several years and very large samples"}
The 1980 survey pools collections from 1978 to 1981, and seven of its samples have more
than 1,000 beetles (Oude Tonge 15,217). These samples were collected over several years
and probably from many trees, whereas the later samples have one or two hundred beetles. A
model that treats every beetle as an independent trial gives the 1980 samples almost all
the weight (@sec-choices).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the number of samples, not of beetles"}
The cline is described by `r nrow(ew)` samples at `r nlevels(ew$site)` localities, not by
`r big(sum(ew$n))` beetles. Beetles of one sample share the place and the year, and pupae
collected from the same tree may be siblings, so they are not independent trials of one
probability given by a smooth curve.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: different localities in different surveys"}
A mean of the proportions per survey compares different sets of localities: Waalre (the
most inland site) is missing in 1995 and 2004, Goedereede (near the coast) in 1980, and
six localities in 2004. A comparison of surveys must account for distance, which the model
does.
:::

## Frequencies along the transect {#sec-transect}

@fig-transect shows the proportion of melanics in each sample against the distance to the
coast, one line per survey.

```{r}
#| label: fig-transect
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of melanics in each sample against the distance to the coast,
#|   one line and symbol per survey (east–west transect)."
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 4.2
plot(prop ~ distance_km, data = ew, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 0.65),
     xlab = "Distance to the coast (km)", ylab = "Proportion of melanics")
for (y in seq_along(levels(ew$year_f))) {
  ew_year = ew[ew$year_f == levels(ew$year_f)[y], ]
  ew_year = ew_year[order(ew_year$distance_km), ]
  lines(prop ~ distance_km, data = ew_year, col = year_colours[y])
  points(prop ~ distance_km, data = ew_year, col = year_colours[y],
         pch = year_symbols[y])
}
legend("bottomright", legend = levels(ew$year_f), col = year_colours,
       pch = year_symbols, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

In 1980 the proportion is about 0.1 to 0.25 within 30 km of the coast, rises steeply
between about 30 and 50 km and stays at about 0.55 further inland: a sigmoid cline with
two plateaus. In the later surveys the coastal samples stay at about 0.15 to 0.25, while
the inland plateau falls (to about 0.45 in 1991, 0.3 to 0.35 in 1995 and 1998, and about
0.25 in 2004), so that the cline becomes lower and by 2004 almost flat. The position of
the rise does not move visibly. Two 1980 samples stand out: Middelharnis (22 km,
`r pct(ew$prop[ew$place == "Middelharnis" & ew$year == 1980])`% of
`r big(ew$n[ew$place == "Middelharnis" & ew$year == 1980])` beetles) lies below every coastal
sample, and Klundert (50 km) lies well below its neighbours.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a cline is not a straight line on the logit scale"}
A logistic regression of the proportion on distance (a GLM or GLMM with `distance` as a
linear predictor of the logit) describes a curve that rises from 0 to 1 without
plateaus. The cline of 1980 has a lower plateau at about 0.15 and an upper one at about
0.55, so a linear predictor must compromise between the steep middle and the flat ends.
@sec-linear compares the two.
:::

## How much do the samples vary? {#sec-variation}

Beyond about 50 km the cline is flat, so the samples there estimate the same frequency in
each survey. If the beetles of all these samples were independent trials with the same
probability, the Pearson chi-square statistic of the samples (the heterogeneity
chi-square of the papers) divided by its degrees of freedom would be about one. We
calculate it per survey, with the standard deviation of the proportions among samples on
the logit scale:

```{r}
plateau = ew[ew$distance_km > 50, ]
plateau_variation = t(sapply(split(plateau, plateau$year), function(s) {
  pooled = sum(s$black) / sum(s$n)
  chisq = sum((s$black - s$n * pooled)^2 / (s$n * pooled * (1 - pooled)))
  c(samples = nrow(s), mean_n = mean(s$n), pooled = pooled,
    chisq_per_df = chisq / (nrow(s) - 1), sd_logit = sd(qlogis(s$prop)))
}))
round(plateau_variation, 2)
```

In 1980 the inland samples differ least on the logit scale
(`r f2(plateau_variation["1980", "sd_logit"])`), and yet their ratio is
`r f1(plateau_variation["1980", "chisq_per_df"])`; in 1995 the ratio is about as large
with samples of a few hundred beetles, because the samples differ more (Tilburg 44%
against Zevenbergen 29% of 770 beetles). In 1998 and 2004 the ratio is below one. One
model explains this pattern: if the probability itself varies among samples with a
standard deviation $\sigma$ on the logit scale, the variance of a proportion is roughly
$p(1-p)/N + \left(p(1-p)\right)^2\sigma^2$, so the same $\sigma$ gives a ratio that grows
with the sample size $N$. With thousands of beetles per sample in 1980, even small
differences among samples dwarf the Binomial variation; with 100 to 200 beetles they are
of similar size or smaller. This is the variance factor $(\kappa+N)/(\kappa+1)$ of the
Beta-Binomial distribution in Chapter 6, and the reason why the model needs variation
among samples. With three to six samples per survey, both statistics are rough, and a
standard deviation of the logit proportions also contains the Binomial variation of the
small samples.

## What we take forward {#sec-forward}

- **The curve:** a sigmoid cline with a lower (coastal) and an upper (inland) plateau.
- **The observations:** the number of melanics out of the beetles of a sample, Binomial
  for a given probability of the sample.
- **The groups:** the probability varies among samples beyond the curve, with a similar
  standard deviation on the logit scale in every survey; a random effect per sample on the
  logit scale (as for the tadpole tanks in the Chapter 7 practical), or a Beta-Binomial
  distribution (Chapter 6). Whether a locality keeps its deviation from one survey to the
  next (a random effect per site) is checked in @sec-choices.
- **The predictor:** the survey, a factor with five levels, enters as a fixed effect on the
  parameters of the cline through model matrices (Chapter 7, `sec-model-matrix`).

# The model {#sec-model}

## The cline

We describe the frequency of melanics at distance $d$ from the coast by a logistic
function with two plateaus:

$$
p(d) = p_{\mathrm{coast}} + \frac{p_{\mathrm{inland}} - p_{\mathrm{coast}}}{1 + e^{-b(d - c)}},
$$

where $p_{\mathrm{coast}}$ is the frequency at the coast (the lower plateau, approached as
$d$ decreases), $p_{\mathrm{inland}}$ the frequency inland (the upper plateau), $c$ the
centre of the cline (km), where the frequency is half-way between the plateaus, and $b$ the
steepness (1/km). It is the logistic function of the functions supplement
(`sec-fn-logistic`, with asymptote $a$, steepness $b$ and midpoint $c$), scaled to
$p_{\mathrm{inland}} - p_{\mathrm{coast}}$ and raised by $p_{\mathrm{coast}}$. Its slope
at the centre is $(p_{\mathrm{inland}} - p_{\mathrm{coast}})\,b/4$, so the **width** of
the cline, the step divided by the largest slope (the usual measure in studies of clines),
is $4/b$ km. The step from 10% to 90% of the way between the plateaus takes
$2\log(9)/b \approx 4.4/b$ km.

The plateaus are probabilities, so we optimise them on the logit scale; the steepness is
positive, so we optimise $\log(b)$; the centre is optimised on its own scale (km). From
@fig-transect: $p_{\mathrm{coast}} \approx 0.15$, $p_{\mathrm{inland}} \approx 0.55$,
$c \approx 40$ km (half-way up the 1980 rise) and a rise over about 25 km, so
$b \approx 4/25 \approx 0.15$/km.

```{r}
library(RTMB)
library(RTMBdist)

cline = function(d, p_coast, p_inland, steepness, centre) {
  p_coast + (p_inland - p_coast) / (1 + exp(-steepness * (d - centre)))
}
```

## The model for the samples

The model for sample $j$ (a locality in a survey) with $N_j$ beetles, of which $Y_j$ are
melanic, is

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{logit}(p_{\mathrm{coast},j}) &= \beta_{\mathrm{coast},0}
  + \beta_{\mathrm{coast},1991}\,T_{1991,j} + \cdots + \beta_{\mathrm{coast},2004}\,T_{2004,j},\\
\operatorname{logit}(p_{\mathrm{inland},j}) &= \beta_{\mathrm{inland},0}
  + \beta_{\mathrm{inland},1991}\,T_{1991,j} + \cdots + \beta_{\mathrm{inland},2004}\,T_{2004,j},\\
u_j &\sim \operatorname{Normal}(0, \sigma^2_{\mathrm{sample}}),\\
\operatorname{logit}(p_j) &= \operatorname{logit}\left(p_{\mathrm{coast},j}
  + \frac{p_{\mathrm{inland},j} - p_{\mathrm{coast},j}}{1 + e^{-b(d_j - c)}}\right) + u_j,\\
Y_j \mid u_j &\sim \operatorname{Binomial}(N_j, p_j),
\end{aligned}
$$

where $T_{1991,j}$ is 1 if sample $j$ comes from the 1991 survey and 0 otherwise (and so
on for the other surveys; 1980 is the reference level), $d_j$ is the distance of its
locality to the coast, and the samples are independent for given $u_j$. The beetles are
the observations and the samples their groups, as the tadpoles and tanks of the Chapter 7
practical. The deviation $u_j$ shifts the probability of sample $j$ on the logit scale,
so the typical frequency of a survey ($u_j = 0$) at a distance is that of its median
sample, which is close to the mean sample when $\sigma_{\mathrm{sample}}$ is small. This
model, with only the plateaus depending on the survey, is the candidate `ends` of
@sec-candidates; the other candidates change which parameters depend on the survey.

The answer is the typical frequency at 10 km and at 60 km from the coast in each survey,
$p(10)$ and $p(60)$ with $u_j = 0$, and the odds ratio between them,

$$
\mathrm{OR} = \frac{p(60)/\left(1 - p(60)\right)}{p(10)/\left(1 - p(10)\right)},
$$

the height of the cline on the odds scale (1 for a flat cline). Both distances lie inside
the sampled range in every survey (localities at 5.6 to 11.6 km and at 55.4 to 64 km).

## Implementation

The list of data holds the counts, the sample sizes, the distances, the index of the
sample (1 to `r nrow(ew)`) and of the site (1 to `r nlevels(ew$site)`) of each row, and the
two distances of the answer. The surveys are a property of each sample, so the model
matrices of the samples come from `ew` itself (one row per sample), and those of the
typical values from `years`, one row per survey.

```{r}
years = data.frame(year_f = factor(levels(ew$year_f), levels = levels(ew$year_f)))
rownames(years) = levels(ew$year_f)
years$decades = (as.numeric(levels(ew$year_f)) - 1980) / 10
ew$decades = (ew$year - 1980) / 10

ew_data = list(black = ew$black, n = ew$n, distance = ew$distance_km,
               sample = seq_len(nrow(ew)), site = as.numeric(ew$site),
               answer_distance = c(10, 60))
```

`decades` (years since 1980, divided by 10) serves the candidates with a trend in
@sec-candidates. One joint NLL covers every model of this document. Two choices are
elements of the list of data:

- `distribution`: `"Binomial"` or `"BetaBinomial"` (with the mean probability $p_j$ and
  the precision $\kappa$, as in Chapter 6);
- `group`: the index of the group of the random effect of each row, the sample or the
  site, or `NULL` for no random effect (`random` is then `"none"`).

`ADREPORT()` gives the logit of the typical frequency at the two distances in each survey
and the log odds ratio between them.

```{r}
cline_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  black = OBS(black)
  nll = 0
  # Minus the log density of the deviations of the groups, before they are used.
  if (random != "none") {
    sd_group = exp(log_sd_group)
    nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = sd_group, log = TRUE))
  }
  # Cline of each sample, and its probability on the logit scale.
  p_coast = plogis(X_coast %*% beta_coast)
  p_inland = plogis(X_inland %*% beta_inland)
  steepness = exp(X_steepness %*% beta_steepness)
  centre = X_centre %*% beta_centre
  logit_p = qlogis(cline(distance, p_coast, p_inland, steepness, centre))
  if (random != "none") {
    logit_p = logit_p + u[group]
  }
  p = plogis(logit_p)
  # Typical frequencies (u = 0) of each survey at the two distances of the answer.
  coast_year = plogis(X_coast_year %*% beta_coast)
  inland_year = plogis(X_inland_year %*% beta_inland)
  steepness_year = exp(X_steepness_year %*% beta_steepness)
  centre_year = X_centre_year %*% beta_centre
  logit_freq_near = qlogis(cline(answer_distance[1], coast_year, inland_year,
                                 steepness_year, centre_year))
  logit_freq_far = qlogis(cline(answer_distance[2], coast_year, inland_year,
                                steepness_year, centre_year))
  log_odds_ratio = logit_freq_far - logit_freq_near
  ADREPORT(logit_freq_near)
  ADREPORT(logit_freq_far)
  ADREPORT(log_odds_ratio)
  # Minus the log probability of the counts for given deviations.
  if (distribution == "Binomial") {
    nll = nll - sum(dbinom(x = black, size = n, prob = p, log = TRUE))
  } else {
    kappa = exp(log_kappa)
    nll = nll - sum(dbetabinom(x = black, size = n, shape1 = kappa * p,
                               shape2 = kappa * (1 - p), log = TRUE))
  }
  nll
}
```

`cline_setup()` builds the list of data and the starting values for a list of formulas
(for the coastal and inland plateaus, the steepness and the centre), a distribution and a
random effect (`"none"`, `"sample"` or `"site"`). The baseline values are those read from
@fig-transect; every effect starts at zero, the standard deviation of the groups at 0.3
(@sec-variation) and the precision at 50. Every fit in this document converged from these
values unless the text says otherwise.

```{r}
cline_setup = function(data, sample_info, years, formulas, distribution, random) {
  data$distribution = distribution
  data$random = random
  for (par in c("coast", "inland", "steepness", "centre")) {
    data[[paste0("X_", par)]] = model.matrix(formulas[[par]], data = sample_info)
    data[[paste0("X_", par, "_year")]] = model.matrix(formulas[[par]], data = years)
  }
  baseline = c(coast = qlogis(0.15), inland = qlogis(0.55),
               steepness = log(0.15), centre = 40)
  start = list()
  for (par in names(baseline)) {
    start[[paste0("beta_", par)]] = c(baseline[[par]],
                                      rep(0, ncol(data[[paste0("X_", par)]]) - 1))
  }
  if (distribution == "BetaBinomial") {
    start$log_kappa = log(50)
  }
  if (random != "none") {
    data$group = data[[random]]
    start$log_sd_group = log(0.3)
    start$u = rep(0, max(data$group))
  }
  list(data = data, start = start)
}
```

Three helpers complete the toolkit:

- `fit_cline()` processes the joint NLL for one list of data, integrating out `u` when
  the model has a random effect, and minimises it;
- `aic_table()` reports, for a named list of fits, $K$, the log-likelihood, the
  convergence code, the largest absolute gradient at the solution, AIC and the difference
  from the lowest AIC;
- `cline_answer()` gives the typical frequency at the two distances in each survey and
  the odds ratio, with Wald intervals calculated on the logit or log scale and
  transformed back.

```{r}
# Connect a likelihood to a data set.
cmb = function(f, d) function(p) f(p, d)

fit_cline = function(data, start) {
  random = if (data$random == "none") NULL else "u"
  obj = MakeADFun(cmb(cline_nll, data), start, random = random, silent = TRUE)
  fit = optim(par = obj$par, fn = obj$fn, gr = obj$gr, method = "BFGS")
  list(obj = obj, fit = fit)
}

aic_table = function(fits) {
  out = data.frame(
    model = names(fits),
    K = sapply(fits, function(f) length(f$fit$par)),
    loglik = sapply(fits, function(f) -f$fit$value),
    convergence = sapply(fits, function(f) f$fit$convergence),
    max_gradient = sapply(fits, function(f) max(abs(f$obj$gr(f$fit$par))))
  )
  out$aic = 2 * out$K - 2 * out$loglik
  out$delta_aic = out$aic - min(out$aic)
  rownames(out) = NULL
  out
}

critical_value = qnorm(p = 0.975)
cline_answer = function(obj, year_names = rownames(years)) {
  report = summary(sdreport(obj), select = "report")
  est = report[, "Estimate"]
  se = report[, "Std. Error"]
  rows = split(seq_along(est), rownames(report))
  back = function(name, f) {
    r = rows[[name]]
    cbind(f(est[r]), f(est[r] - critical_value * se[r]),
          f(est[r] + critical_value * se[r]))
  }
  out = data.frame(year = year_names,
                   back("logit_freq_near", plogis), back("logit_freq_far", plogis),
                   back("log_odds_ratio", exp))
  names(out)[-1] = paste(rep(c("near", "far", "odds_ratio"), each = 3),
                         c("estimate", "lower", "upper"), sep = "_")
  out
}

# Print an AIC table or an answer table in the document.
show_table = function(tab, digits = 2) {
  if ("max_gradient" %in% names(tab)) {
    tab$max_gradient = format(signif(tab$max_gradient, 2))
  }
  knitr::kable(tab, digits = digits, row.names = FALSE)
}
```

In `cline_answer()`, "near" is the first distance of the answer (10 km) and "far" the
second (60 km).

# Which distribution, which random effect? {#sec-choices}

The full model, in which the survey changes every parameter of the cline, cannot be
fitted reliably (@sec-candidates), so the choices are compared with the candidate `ends`,
in which both plateaus depend on the survey and the centre and steepness are shared. We
compare a Binomial and a Beta-Binomial distribution, each without a random effect and with
a random effect per site, and the Binomial distribution with a random effect per sample.
(A Beta-Binomial distribution with a random effect per sample would describe the same
variation twice.)

```{r}
ends_formulas = list(coast = ~ year_f, inland = ~ year_f, steepness = ~ 1,
                     centre = ~ 1)

choices = data.frame(
  distribution = c("Binomial", "Binomial", "Binomial", "BetaBinomial", "BetaBinomial"),
  random = c("none", "site", "sample", "none", "site")
)
choice_setups = list()
choice_fits = list()
for (i in seq_len(nrow(choices))) {
  choice_setups[[i]] = cline_setup(ew_data, ew, years, ends_formulas,
                                   choices$distribution[i], choices$random[i])
  choice_fits[[i]] = fit_cline(choice_setups[[i]]$data, choice_setups[[i]]$start)
}
names(choice_fits) = paste(choices$distribution, choices$random)
choice_table = aic_table(choice_fits)
show_table(choice_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Quantities quoted in the text.
aic_choice = setNames(choice_table$aic, choice_table$model)
delta_choice = setNames(choice_table$delta_aic, choice_table$model)
sd_site_bb = exp(choice_fits[["BetaBinomial site"]]$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
sd_sample = exp(choice_fits[["Binomial sample"]]$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
sd_site_bin = exp(choice_fits[["Binomial site"]]$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
kappa_bb = exp(choice_fits[["BetaBinomial none"]]$fit$par[["log_kappa"]])
```

`r if (all(choice_table$convergence == 0)) "All five fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
The Binomial model without a random effect is worse than the best by
`r round(delta_choice[["Binomial none"]])` AIC units, and a random effect per site improves
it a lot but not enough (still `r round(delta_choice[["Binomial site"]])` units behind).
The random effect per sample and the Beta-Binomial distribution describe the same thing,
a probability that varies among samples around the cline, with a logit-Normal
distribution in one and a Beta distribution in the other; the Beta-Binomial model is
better by `r f1(aic_choice[["Binomial sample"]] - aic_choice[["BetaBinomial none"]])` AIC
units with the same $K$. The estimated standard deviation among samples is
`r f2(sd_sample)` on the logit scale, and the precision of the Beta-Binomial model is
`r round(kappa_bb)`.

Adding a random effect per site to the Beta-Binomial model does not improve it at all:
the standard deviation among sites goes to `r signif(sd_site_bb, 2)`, practically zero, and
the log-likelihood is that of the model without it. Once the samples may vary, the
localities show no deviation that persists from one survey to the next (@sec-two-re
confirms this with both random effects).

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a random effect per site is the obvious choice and the wrong one"}
The localities are the obvious groups: the same 16 places were sampled repeatedly. But a
random effect per site describes deviations that a locality keeps in every survey, and the
data show none; what varies is the sample. With a Binomial distribution, the random
effect per site absorbs part of the variation among samples (standard deviation
`r f2(sd_site_bin)` on the logit scale), which still leaves the large 1980 samples far
from the curve, and the fit is `r round(aic_choice[["Binomial site"]] - aic_choice[["Binomial sample"]])`
AIC units worse than with a random effect per sample. With a Beta-Binomial distribution
the variance among sites goes to zero, an estimate at the boundary of its range: the fit
reports convergence, and only the estimate shows the problem ($\log(\sigma_{\mathrm{site}})$
far below any plausible value, so a Wald interval of it is meaningless; Chapter 8
material).
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the Binomial model without variation among samples"}
The estimates of the Binomial model without a random effect, next to those with a random
effect per sample (on the optimised scales):

```{r}
binomial_fixed = summary(sdreport(choice_fits[["Binomial none"]]$obj), select = "fixed")
sample_fixed = summary(sdreport(choice_fits[["Binomial sample"]]$obj), select = "fixed")
# The parameters are in the same order; the random effect adds log_sd_group at the end.
round(cbind(binomial_fixed, sample_fixed[seq_len(nrow(binomial_fixed)), ]), 3)
```

Without the random effect, the few samples of several thousand beetles decide the curve:
the coastal plateau of 1980 is pulled down to
`r pct(plogis(binomial_fixed[1, "Estimate"]))`% (against
`r pct(plogis(sample_fixed[1, "Estimate"]))`% with the random effect) by the 8,256 beetles
of Middelharnis (9%), and the centre moves from
`r f1(sample_fixed["beta_centre", "Estimate"])` to
`r f1(binomial_fixed["beta_centre", "Estimate"])` km with a standard error about
`r round(sample_fixed["beta_centre", "Std. Error"] / binomial_fixed["beta_centre", "Std. Error"])`
times smaller. The standard errors of the inland plateaus are about two to five times
smaller,
whereas those of the coastal plateaus are larger, because the coastal samples disagree
with a curve that the large inland samples have fixed. The model treats 15,217 beetles
from Oude Tonge as 15,217 independent trials of the probability given by the curve.
:::

We continue with the Binomial model with a random effect per sample, a non-linear mixed
model of Chapter 7, although the Beta-Binomial model has the lower AIC. The two describe
the same variation and give the same answer (@sec-sensitivity); the mixed model is the
subject of the case study, and with it the random effect per sample and the random effect
per site are alternatives of the same kind, which students can compare directly.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Use the Beta-Binomial model throughout (no random effect, so no Laplace approximation),
and add the random effect per site to show that it collapses. Its $p_j$ is the mean
frequency of the samples at a distance, not that of the median sample.
:::

# Is the cline non-linear? {#sec-linear}

A model that a student could fit with `glmmTMB` lets the logit of the probability depend
linearly on the distance, with an intercept and a slope per survey and a random effect per
sample:
$\operatorname{logit}(p_j) = \beta_{0,y(j)} + \beta_{1,y(j)}\,d_j + u_j$. We write it as
its own short NLL.

```{r}
linear_nll = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  black = OBS(black)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_group), log = TRUE))
  logit_p = X_year %*% beta_intercept + (X_year %*% beta_slope) * distance + u[sample]
  nll - sum(dbinom(x = black, size = n, prob = plogis(logit_p), log = TRUE))
}
linear_data = ew_data
linear_data$X_year = model.matrix(~ year_f - 1, data = ew)
linear_start = list(beta_intercept = rep(qlogis(0.15), 5), beta_slope = rep(0, 5),
                    log_sd_group = log(0.3), u = rep(0, nrow(ew)))
linear_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(linear_nll, linear_data), linear_start, random = "u",
                       silent = TRUE)
linear_fit = optim(par = linear_obj$par, fn = linear_obj$fn, gr = linear_obj$gr,
                   method = "BFGS")
linear_table = aic_table(list(
  cline_ends = choice_fits[["Binomial sample"]],
  linear = list(obj = linear_obj, fit = linear_fit)
))
show_table(linear_table, digits = 1)
```

The cline with plateaus is better by
`r round(linear_table$aic[2] - linear_table$aic[1])` AIC units with
`r linear_table$K[1] - linear_table$K[2]` parameters more. The linear predictor (a
separate intercept and slope per survey, `~ year_f - 1` in the model matrix) cannot have
the plateaus of 1980, and its estimate of the variation among samples is larger
(`r f2(exp(linear_fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]))` against `r f2(sd_sample)` on the logit
scale) because the misfit of the curve is put into the samples.

**Teaching point.** This is the motivation of the course for non-linear models: the
parameters of the cline (frequencies at the coast and inland, centre, width) are the ones
that ecologists report and the ones that the research question is about, and the linear
predictor has none of them.

# How did the cline change? {#sec-candidates}

With the Binomial distribution and a random effect per sample, the candidates differ in
the parameters that depend on the survey:

- `none`: one cline for all surveys;
- `coast`, `inland`: only one plateau changes;
- `ends`: both plateaus change (the main model of @sec-model);
- `ends_centre`, `ends_steepness`: both plateaus and the centre or the steepness change;
- `inland_trend`: the logit of the inland plateau changes linearly with time (one
  parameter per decade instead of four survey effects), the coast stays.

```{r}
candidates = list(
  none = list(coast = ~ 1, inland = ~ 1, steepness = ~ 1, centre = ~ 1),
  coast = list(coast = ~ year_f, inland = ~ 1, steepness = ~ 1, centre = ~ 1),
  inland = list(coast = ~ 1, inland = ~ year_f, steepness = ~ 1, centre = ~ 1),
  ends = ends_formulas,
  ends_centre = list(coast = ~ year_f, inland = ~ year_f, steepness = ~ 1,
                     centre = ~ year_f),
  ends_steepness = list(coast = ~ year_f, inland = ~ year_f, steepness = ~ year_f,
                        centre = ~ 1),
  inland_trend = list(coast = ~ 1, inland = ~ decades, steepness = ~ 1, centre = ~ 1)
)
candidate_setups = list()
candidate_fits = list()
for (m in names(candidates)) {
  candidate_setups[[m]] = cline_setup(ew_data, ew, years, candidates[[m]],
                                      "Binomial", "sample")
  candidate_fits[[m]] = fit_cline(candidate_setups[[m]]$data,
                                  candidate_setups[[m]]$start)
}
candidate_table = aic_table(candidate_fits)
show_table(candidate_table, digits = 1)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_cand = setNames(candidate_table$delta_aic, candidate_table$model)
```

`r if (all(candidate_table$convergence == 0)) "All seven fits converged." else "Not every fit converged (see the table)."`
A single cline for all surveys (`none`) is worse than the best by
`r round(delta_cand[["none"]])` AIC units, and a change of the coastal plateau alone
(`coast`) does not help at all: its log-likelihood is
`r f1(candidate_table$loglik[2] - candidate_table$loglik[1])` units higher for four more
parameters. A change of the
inland plateau carries almost all of the improvement: `inland` is
`r f1(delta_cand[["inland"]])` units behind the best, and letting the coastal plateau
change as well (`ends`) costs `r f1(delta_cand[["ends"]] - delta_cand[["inland"]])` units.
A centre or a steepness per survey does not improve `ends`
(`r f1(delta_cand[["ends_centre"]] - delta_cand[["ends"]])` and
`r f1(delta_cand[["ends_steepness"]] - delta_cand[["ends"]])` units more). The trend model
is `r if (delta_cand[["inland_trend"]] == 0) "the best" else paste(f1(delta_cand[["inland_trend"]]), "units behind the best")`:
a steady decline of the inland plateau on the logit scale describes the five surveys as
well as a separate value for each.

The answer uses `ends`, in which both plateaus can change, because the question asks which
end of the cline changed; with `inland`, the constancy of the coast would be an assumption
and not a result. AIC shows that this freedom costs little and that the data give no
reason to let the cline move or change its width.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: the centre and the width of a flat cline"}
When the two plateaus are close, the centre and the steepness hardly change the curve, so
the data cannot estimate them. The full model, with every parameter of the cline
depending on the survey:

```{r}
full_formulas = list(coast = ~ year_f, inland = ~ year_f, steepness = ~ year_f,
                     centre = ~ year_f)
full_setup = cline_setup(ew_data, ew, years, full_formulas, "Binomial", "sample")
full_fit = fit_cline(full_setup$data, full_setup$start)
full_fit$fit$convergence
max(abs(full_fit$obj$gr(full_fit$fit$par)))
full_fixed = summary(sdreport(full_fit$obj), select = "fixed")
round(full_fixed[grepl("steepness|centre", rownames(full_fixed)), ], 2)
```

`optim()` stops at its limit of iterations (convergence code
`r full_fit$fit$convergence`) with a gradient far from zero, and the effects of the later
surveys on the centre have standard errors as large as or larger than the effects
themselves (`r round(max(full_fixed[grepl("centre", rownames(full_fixed)), "Std. Error"]))`
km at the most). The steepness of the 1995 and 2004 clines and their centres are hardly
constrained, because their plateaus are close. The parameters of the shape of a cline are
only defined while the cline exists, which is why `ends` shares them across surveys. This
is practical non-identifiability (Chapter 8).
:::

# The answer: frequencies at the coast and inland {#sec-answer}

We take the candidate `ends` and calculate its `sdreport()`.

```{r}
ends_data = candidate_setups$ends$data
ends_start = candidate_setups$ends$start
ends = candidate_fits$ends
ends_obj = ends$obj
ends_fit = ends$fit
ends_fit$convergence
ends_sd = sdreport(ends_obj)
```

The typical frequency of melanics at 10 km ("near") and 60 km ("far") from the coast in
each survey, and the odds ratio between them, with 95% Wald intervals:

```{r}
ends_answer = cline_answer(ends_obj)
show_table(ends_answer)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
# Estimate and interval of a column group of row r of an answer table, in percent.
answer_pct = function(tab, what, r) {
  paste0(pct(tab[r, paste0(what, "_estimate")]), "% (",
         pct(tab[r, paste0(what, "_lower")]), " to ",
         pct(tab[r, paste0(what, "_upper")]), "%)")
}
answer_or = function(tab, r) {
  paste0(f2(tab$odds_ratio_estimate[r]), " (", f2(tab$odds_ratio_lower[r]), " to ",
         f2(tab$odds_ratio_upper[r]), ")")
}
```

At 60 km from the coast, the typical frequency of melanics fell from
`r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 1)` in 1980 to `r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 2)` in
1991, `r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 3)` in 1995, `r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 4)`
in 1998 and `r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 5)` in 2004. At 10 km it stayed between
`r pct(min(ends_answer$near_estimate))`% and `r pct(max(ends_answer$near_estimate))`%,
with intervals that overlap in every survey. The odds ratio between 60 and 10 km, the
height of the cline, fell from `r answer_or(ends_answer, 1)` in 1980 to
`r answer_or(ends_answer, 5)` in 2004. The cline did not move; it became lower because the
inland populations lost melanics, and by 2004 the difference between coast and inland is
`r if (ends_answer$odds_ratio_lower[5] > 1) "small but still clear" else "within the uncertainty of the data"`.

The difference in percentage points between 60 and 10 km (point estimates only; an
interval for a difference of probabilities should come from a transformed scale, as for
the odds ratio):

```{r}
height_points = 100 * (ends_answer$far_estimate - ends_answer$near_estimate)
names(height_points) = ends_answer$year
round(height_points, 1)
```

::: {.callout-note title="Comparison with the papers (for the author)"}
Brakefield and de Jong (2011, Figure 2b) summarise the height of the cline as the
difference between the median percentage of melanics of the five most westerly and the
five most easterly localities: about 40 points in 1980 and about 4 in 2004 (read from
the figure). Their medians use whichever localities were sampled, so they do not refer to
fixed distances, but the pattern agrees with the differences above. Their statistical
analysis is a general linear model of the arcsine-square-root transformed percentages
with survey as a factor and distance as a linear covariate, which gives every sample the
same weight (35 or 15,217 beetles) and cannot describe the plateaus; it reports
significant effects of survey and distance. They also note that the 2004 samples are
heterogeneous mainly because of Goedereede (8.6%, 13 of 152). The 1998 paper fits the
curves by eye and tests the change at each locality with chi-square tests. Neither paper
estimates the parameters of the cline. The results should not be given to students
before they analyse the data.
:::

The estimates on the optimised scales, labelled by parameter and column of the model
matrix:

```{r}
ends_fixed = summary(ends_sd, select = "fixed")
rownames(ends_fixed) = c(paste0("coast_", colnames(ends_data$X_coast)),
                         paste0("inland_", colnames(ends_data$X_inland)),
                         "log_steepness", "centre", "log_sd_sample")
round(ends_fixed, 3)
```

The typical plateaus of each survey on the original scale, and the shared centre (km),
steepness (1/km) and width $4/b$ (km):

```{r}
ends_par = split(ends_fit$par, names(ends_fit$par))
year_plateaus = data.frame(
  coast = plogis(ends_data$X_coast_year %*% ends_par$beta_coast),
  inland = plogis(ends_data$X_inland_year %*% ends_par$beta_inland),
  row.names = rownames(years)
)
round(year_plateaus, 3)
steepness_ends = exp(ends_par$beta_steepness)
centre_ends = ends_par$beta_centre
c(centre = centre_ends, steepness = steepness_ends, width = 4 / steepness_ends)
```

The centre lies `r f1(centre_ends)` km from the coast (standard error
`r f1(ends_fixed["centre", "Std. Error"])` km) and the width is
`r round(4 / steepness_ends)` km. The inland plateau, which lies beyond about
`r round(centre_ends + 2.2 / steepness_ends)` km (where 90% of the step is reached),
fell from `r pct(year_plateaus$inland[1])`% to `r pct(year_plateaus$inland[5])`%; the
coastal plateau stayed between `r pct(min(year_plateaus$coast))`% and
`r pct(max(year_plateaus$coast))`%. The plateaus are close to the frequencies at 10 and
60 km, as they should be for a cline whose rise lies between the two distances.

The standard deviation among samples, with a likelihood profile interval (calculated on
the log scale and transformed back):

```{r}
ends_profile_sd = TMB::tmbprofile(ends_obj, name = "log_sd_group", trace = FALSE)
sd_sample_ci = exp(c(estimate = ends_fit$par[["log_sd_group"]],
                     confint(ends_profile_sd)[1, ]))
sd_sample_ci
```

The probability of a sample varies around the cline with a standard deviation of
`r f2(sd_sample_ci[1])` on the logit scale (profile interval `r f2(sd_sample_ci[2])` to
`r f2(sd_sample_ci[3])`). At a frequency of 0.3, a deviation of one standard deviation
changes the frequency by about `r round(100 * 0.3 * 0.7 * sd_sample_ci[1])` percentage
points ($p(1-p)\sigma$), so samples at the same distance in the same survey typically
differ by a few percentage points: much more than the Binomial variation of a sample of
thousands, and comparable with that of a sample of 150 (about
`r round(100 * sqrt(0.3 * 0.7 / 150))` points).

@fig-typical shows the typical clines of the five surveys over the samples.

```{r}
#| label: fig-typical
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of melanics in each sample (points) and typical clines (u = 0)
#|   of the five surveys under the model `ends`, one panel per survey. The dotted lines
#|   mark 10 and 60 km."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 4.8
distance_grid = seq(from = 0, to = 120, length.out = 241)
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(2, 3), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
for (y in seq_along(levels(ew$year_f))) {
  ew_year = ew[ew$year_f == levels(ew$year_f)[y], ]
  plot(prop ~ distance_km, data = ew_year, xlim = c(0, 120), ylim = c(0, 0.65),
       col = year_colours[y], pch = year_symbols[y], main = levels(ew$year_f)[y],
       xlab = "Distance to the coast (km)", ylab = "Proportion of melanics")
  lines(distance_grid, cline(distance_grid, year_plateaus$coast[y],
                             year_plateaus$inland[y], steepness_ends, centre_ends),
        lwd = 2)
  abline(v = c(10, 60), lty = 3, col = "grey50")
}
par(old_par)
```

The typical clines pass through the middle of the samples in every survey. The 1980 rise
between 30 and 50 km is steep, and the two low samples of 1980 (Middelharnis and Klundert)
lie below the curve; the later clines are lower versions of the same shape.

## A steady decline? {#sec-trend}

The candidate `inland_trend` summarises the change as a constant rate on the logit scale.
Its estimates:

```{r}
trend = candidate_fits$inland_trend
trend_fixed = summary(sdreport(trend$obj), select = "fixed")
rownames(trend_fixed) = c("coast", "inland_1980", "inland_per_decade",
                          "log_steepness", "centre", "log_sd_sample")
round(trend_fixed, 3)
trend_factor = exp(trend_fixed["inland_per_decade", "Estimate"] +
                     c(estimate = 0, lower = -1, upper = 1) * critical_value *
                     trend_fixed["inland_per_decade", "Std. Error"])
trend_factor
```

Under this model the odds of a melanic inland were multiplied by
`r f2(trend_factor[1])` per decade (95% Wald interval `r f2(trend_factor[2])` to
`r f2(trend_factor[3])`), while the coastal plateau stayed at
`r pct(plogis(trend_fixed["coast", "Estimate"]))`%. Brakefield and de Jong (2011) turn a
decline from 55 to 20% over about 50 generations into a selection coefficient against
melanics of 0.036 with a population-genetic model; that calculation is beyond this course,
but the trend parameter is the statistical counterpart of the rate that it needs.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative"}
Report the trend model as the answer: one parameter for the rate of change, with a
likelihood profile interval (`TMB::tmbprofile()` of the third element of `beta_inland`).
It assumes a steady change on the logit scale; the AIC table shows that the data do not
contradict it.
:::

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: a change over time is not a test of the climate"}
The data contain the survey years and not the climate. The papers relate the decay of the
cline to warmer and sunnier springs inland (thermal melanism), but any other change
between 1980 and 2004 that affected the inland populations more than the coastal ones
(gene flow, predators, parasites, land use) would produce the same pattern. A model of
these data can describe how the cline changed and how fast; it cannot show why.
:::

# Checking the model {#sec-checks}

## Scaled quantile residuals {#sec-residuals}

We simulate 1,000 hypothetical samples (new deviations of the samples, then new counts
for them) and compare each count with the typical cline of its survey at its distance.
Every sample is a group of one row, so the residuals are residuals of samples.

```{r}
n_sim = 1000
ew_simulations = matrix(NA, nrow = nrow(ew), ncol = n_sim)
set.seed(seed = 1984)
for (s in seq_len(n_sim)) {
  ew_simulations[, s] = ends_obj$simulate(ends_fit$par)$black
}

year_of_sample = as.numeric(ew$year_f)
ew_expected = ew$n * cline(ew$distance_km, year_plateaus$coast[year_of_sample],
                           year_plateaus$inland[year_of_sample], steepness_ends,
                           centre_ends)

ew_residuals = DHARMa::createDHARMa(
  simulatedResponse = ew_simulations,
  observedResponse = ew$black,
  fittedPredictedResponse = ew_expected,
  integerResponse = TRUE
)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals of the model `ends`: quantile-quantile plot (left)
#|   and residuals against the expected number of melanics (right)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 5
plot(ew_residuals)
dispersion_ends = DHARMa::testDispersion(ew_residuals, plot = FALSE)$statistic
dispersion_ends
```

The quantile-quantile plot follows the line, and the residuals show no trend against the
(rank-transformed) predictions. @fig-dharma-distance shows the residuals against the
distance and the survey.

```{r}
#| label: fig-dharma-distance
#| fig-cap: "Scaled quantile residuals against the distance to the coast (left) and the
#|   survey (right)."
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
old_par = par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))
DHARMa::plotResiduals(ew_residuals, form = ew$distance_km, rank = FALSE)
DHARMa::plotResiduals(ew_residuals, form = ew$year_f)
par(old_par)
```

The residuals of the samples (one per sample, the lowest and the highest):

```{r}
sample_scaled = residuals(ew_residuals)
names(sample_scaled) = paste(ew$place, ew$year)
round(head(sort(sample_scaled), 4), 3)
round(tail(sort(sample_scaled), 4), 3)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
n_extreme = sum(sample_scaled < 0.025 | sample_scaled > 0.975)
```

Against the distance, the upper quartile of the residuals lies a little above 0.75 near the
coast (DHARMa draws it in red): the coastal samples are more often above the typical cline
than the model expects, which suggests that the coastal plateau is slightly too low,
pulled down by the low samples of Middelharnis and Dirksland. The surveys look similar.
`r n_extreme` of the `r nrow(ew)` samples have a residual below 0.025 or above 0.975,
against about `r round(0.05 * nrow(ew), 1)` expected; the two lowest are the low 1980
samples of Middelharnis and Klundert. As in Chapter 6, the p-values that DHARMa prints on
its plots are not used for decisions: they test exact agreement, not whether the
disagreement matters for the question.

The dispersion statistic is `r f2(dispersion_ends)`. It compares squared deviations of
counts, so the largest samples dominate it. The share of each sample in the squared
deviations of the observed counts from the mean of the simulations, and the same ratio
of observed to simulated variance on the logit scale of the proportions:

```{r}
sim_mean = rowMeans(ew_simulations)
squared_deviation = (ew$black - sim_mean)^2
share = squared_deviation / sum(squared_deviation)
names(share) = paste(ew$place, ew$year)
round(sort(share, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3], 2)

# Simulated proportions on the logit scale, kept away from 0 and 1.
logit_simulated = qlogis(pmin(pmax(ew_simulations / ew$n, 1e-4), 1 - 1e-4))
dispersion_logit = sum((qlogis(ew$prop) - rowMeans(logit_simulated))^2) /
  sum(apply(logit_simulated, 1, var))
dispersion_logit
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
top_share = sort(share, decreasing = TRUE)
```

`r names(top_share)[1]` and `r names(top_share)[2]`, the two largest samples, account for
`r pct(sum(top_share[1:2]))`% of the squared deviations. On the logit scale, where every
sample counts alike, the ratio is `r f2(dispersion_logit)`: the samples vary around the
typical clines about as much as the model expects. As in the analysis of the
infiltration data, read DHARMa's dispersion statistic with care when the groups differ
this much in size.

## Do localities keep their deviation? {#sec-site-residuals}

One residual per locality, from the sum of its counts over the surveys, shows whether a
locality is consistently above or below the cline (which the random effect per site
would describe):

```{r}
site_residuals = DHARMa::recalculateResiduals(ew_residuals, group = ew_data$site)
site_scaled = residuals(site_residuals)
names(site_scaled) = levels(ew$site)
round(sort(site_scaled), 3)
```

The sums are dominated by the large 1980 samples, so a locality with a low 1980 sample
(Middelharnis, Klundert) has a low residual whatever happened later. The deviations of
the samples of one locality in successive surveys:

```{r}
ends_random = summary(ends_sd, select = "random")
sample_effects = xtabs(ends_random[, "Estimate"] ~ ew$site + ew$year)
sample_effects[sample_sizes == 0] = NA
round(sample_effects, 2)
site_cor = cor(sample_effects[, "1991"], sample_effects[, "1995"],
               use = "complete.obs")
site_cor
```

The predicted effects of the samples (logit scale) are small after 1980 and of varying
sign at most localities; a few keep their sign (Stellendam above the cline, Dirksland
below it), with effects of 0.1 to 0.2. The correlation between the 1991 and 1995 effects
of the same localities is `r f2(site_cor)`. This is the same conclusion as the collapse of
the random effect per site in @sec-choices. Note that predicted effects of small samples are
shrunk towards zero (Chapter 7), so a table of them understates the variation among
samples.

## Sensitivity of the answer {#sec-sensitivity}

The answer (the odds ratio between 60 and 10 km in each survey) under four variants: the
main model, the Beta-Binomial model of @sec-choices, the main model fitted to the 67
samples of the spreadsheet only (without the three samples added from Table 1 of the 2011
paper, see `README.md`), and the model with a centre per survey (`ends_centre`).

```{r}
subset_rows = function(data, rows) {
  for (name in c("black", "n", "distance", "sample", "site")) {
    data[[name]] = data[[name]][rows]
  }
  for (name in grep("^X_[a-z]+$", names(data), value = TRUE)) {
    data[[name]] = data[[name]][rows, , drop = FALSE]
  }
  data$sample = seq_along(rows)
  if (data$random != "none") {
    data$group = data$sample
  }
  data
}
from_table_1 = (ew$place == "Oudenbosch") | (ew$place == "Waalre" & ew$year == 1998)
spreadsheet_data = subset_rows(ends_data, which(!from_table_1))
spreadsheet_start = ends_start
spreadsheet_start$u = rep(0, sum(!from_table_1))
spreadsheet_fit = fit_cline(spreadsheet_data, spreadsheet_start)
spreadsheet_fit$fit$convergence

betabinomial_fit = choice_fits[["BetaBinomial none"]]
sensitivity = data.frame(
  year = ends_answer$year,
  main = ends_answer$odds_ratio_estimate,
  beta_binomial = cline_answer(betabinomial_fit$obj)$odds_ratio_estimate,
  spreadsheet = cline_answer(spreadsheet_fit$obj)$odds_ratio_estimate,
  centre_per_survey = cline_answer(candidate_fits$ends_centre$obj)$odds_ratio_estimate
)
show_table(sensitivity)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
sens_range = apply(sensitivity[, -1], 1, range)
```

The odds ratios agree closely under the four variants (in 1980 between
`r f2(sens_range[1, 1])` and `r f2(sens_range[2, 1])`, in 2004 between
`r f2(sens_range[1, 5])` and `r f2(sens_range[2, 5])`), much closer than their intervals.
The three samples from Table 1 do not change the answer.

# The north–south transect {#sec-ns}

The second transect runs south from Delft, near the coast, and was sampled in 1980 and in
1991 (the 1998 paper says 1992); one locality (Numansdorp) was sampled again in 2004. The
distance is measured from Delft, so it is not the distance to the coast of the east–west
transect and the two clines cannot be compared position by position. Willemstad is a
locality of both transects, and its 1980 sample is the same sample in both (2,565 melanics
and 3,144 non-melanics).

```{r}
ns = adalia[adalia$transect == "NS" & adalia$year < 2000, ]
rownames(ns) = NULL
ns$n = ns$black + ns$red
ns$prop = ns$black / ns$n
ns$site = factor(ns$place, levels = unique(ns$place[order(ns$distance_km)]))
ns$year_f = factor(ns$year)
xtabs(n ~ site + year, data = ns)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ns
#| fig-cap: "Proportion of melanics in each sample of the north–south transect against
#|   the distance from Delft, 1980 and 1991."
#| fig-width: 6
#| fig-height: 4
plot(prop ~ distance_km, data = ns, type = "n", ylim = c(0, 0.65),
     xlab = "Distance from Delft (km)", ylab = "Proportion of melanics")
for (y in 1:2) {
  ns_year = ns[ns$year_f == levels(ns$year_f)[y], ]
  ns_year = ns_year[order(ns_year$distance_km), ]
  lines(prop ~ distance_km, data = ns_year, col = year_colours[y])
  points(prop ~ distance_km, data = ns_year, col = year_colours[y],
         pch = year_symbols[y])
}
legend("bottomright", legend = levels(ns$year_f), col = year_colours[1:2],
       pch = year_symbols[1:2], lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

In 1980 the proportion rises from about 0.03 at Delft to about 0.45 to 0.55 beyond 35 km;
in 1991 the samples near Delft are higher (0.07 to 0.16) and those beyond 35 km mostly
lower. The last locality, Antwerpen (Belgium, 86.5 km), lies 30 km beyond the others.

The same model with 5 km and 45 km from Delft as the distances of the answer (both inside
the sampled range in both surveys), the same baseline values, and the candidates `none`,
`coast`, `inland` and `ends`:

```{r}
ns_years = data.frame(year_f = factor(levels(ns$year_f), levels = levels(ns$year_f)))
rownames(ns_years) = levels(ns$year_f)
ns_data = list(black = ns$black, n = ns$n, distance = ns$distance_km,
               sample = seq_len(nrow(ns)), site = as.numeric(ns$site),
               answer_distance = c(5, 45))
ns_fits = list()
for (m in c("none", "coast", "inland", "ends")) {
  setup = cline_setup(ns_data, ns, ns_years, candidates[[m]], "Binomial", "sample")
  ns_fits[[m]] = fit_cline(setup$data, setup$start)
}
ns_table = aic_table(ns_fits)
show_table(ns_table, digits = 1)
ns_answer = cline_answer(ns_fits$ends$obj, year_names = rownames(ns_years))
show_table(ns_answer)
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
delta_ns = setNames(ns_table$delta_aic, ns_table$model)
```

On this transect the change is at the coastal end: `coast` is
`r f1(delta_ns[["coast"]])` AIC units from the best and `inland`
`r f1(delta_ns[["inland"]])`. Under `ends`, the typical frequency 5 km from Delft rose
from `r answer_pct(ns_answer, "near", 1)` to `r answer_pct(ns_answer, "near", 2)`, and
45 km from Delft it changed from `r answer_pct(ns_answer, "far", 1)` to
`r answer_pct(ns_answer, "far", 2)`. The odds ratio between the two distances fell from
`r answer_or(ns_answer, 1)` to `r answer_or(ns_answer, 2)`. Both clines became shallower,
the east–west one because melanics declined inland and this one mainly because they
increased near Delft. This agrees with the 1998 paper, which reports significant
increases at some western localities and decreases in the south-east.

::: {.callout-tip title="Alternative: one model for both transects"}
Fit both transects in one model, with plateaus per transect and survey and a centre and
steepness per transect, and ask whether the change between 1980 and 1991 is the same on
both. The distances have different origins, so only the plateaus can be compared. The
Willemstad sample of 1980 must then be used once, not twice.
:::

# Beyond the course: deviations of sites and of samples {#sec-two-re}

Chapter 7 uses one random effect per group. Here the samples get a deviation $u_j$
(standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{sample}}$) and the localities a deviation $v_s$
(standard deviation $\sigma_{\mathrm{site}}$), nested: the samples of a locality share
its $v_s$.

```{r}
cline_nll_2re = function(parms, data) {
  getAll(parms, data)
  black = OBS(black)
  nll = -sum(dnorm(x = u, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_sample), log = TRUE))
  nll = nll - sum(dnorm(x = v, mean = 0, sd = exp(log_sd_site), log = TRUE))
  p_coast = plogis(X_coast %*% beta_coast)
  p_inland = plogis(X_inland %*% beta_inland)
  logit_p = qlogis(cline(distance, p_coast, p_inland, exp(beta_steepness),
                         beta_centre)) + u[sample] + v[site]
  nll - sum(dbinom(x = black, size = n, prob = plogis(logit_p), log = TRUE))
}
start_2re = ends_start
start_2re$log_sd_group = NULL
start_2re$log_sd_sample = log(0.3)
start_2re$log_sd_site = log(0.3)
start_2re$u = rep(0, nrow(ew))
start_2re$v = rep(0, nlevels(ew$site))
obj_2re = MakeADFun(cmb(cline_nll_2re, ends_data), start_2re, random = c("u", "v"),
                    silent = TRUE)
fit_2re = optim(par = obj_2re$par, fn = obj_2re$fn, gr = obj_2re$gr, method = "BFGS")
table_2re = aic_table(list(sample_only = ends,
                           sample_and_site = list(obj = obj_2re, fit = fit_2re)))
show_table(table_2re, digits = 1)
sd_2re = exp(fit_2re$par[c("log_sd_sample", "log_sd_site")])
sd_2re
```

The standard deviation among localities goes to `r signif(sd_2re[2], 2)` and that among
samples stays at `r f2(sd_2re[1])`: the localities show no persistent deviation, and the
model with both random effects is worse by the two units of its extra parameter. The
correlation between the deviations of a locality in successive surveys, which ecologists
might expect from local adaptation or a lasting local climate, is not supported by these
data.

# Checking the estimator by simulation {#sec-simulation}

We draw 300 hypothetical samples of the 70 samples from the fitted model `ends` (same
localities, surveys and numbers of beetles) and fit each from the same starting values as
the data. We keep the log odds ratios between 60 and 10 km (estimates and standard
errors) and the standard deviation among samples.

```{r}
set.seed(seed = 2011)
n_samples = 300
sim_log_or = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 5)
sim_se = matrix(NA, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 5)
sim_sd_sample = rep(NA, n_samples)
n_failed = 0
for (i in seq_len(n_samples)) {
  sim_data = ends_data
  sim_data$black = ends_obj$simulate(ends_fit$par)$black
  sim = fit_cline(sim_data, ends_start)
  n_failed = n_failed + (sim$fit$convergence != 0)
  sim_report = summary(sdreport(sim$obj), select = "report")
  or_rows = rownames(sim_report) == "log_odds_ratio"
  sim_log_or[i, ] = sim_report[or_rows, "Estimate"]
  sim_se[i, ] = sim_report[or_rows, "Std. Error"]
  sim_sd_sample[i] = exp(sim$fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
}
n_failed
```

The bias, the standard deviation of the estimates, the mean standard error and the
coverage of the 95% Wald interval for the log odds ratio of each survey:

```{r}
ends_report = summary(ends_sd, select = "report")
log_or_used = ends_report[rownames(ends_report) == "log_odds_ratio", "Estimate"]
log_or_matrix = matrix(log_or_used, nrow = n_samples, ncol = 5, byrow = TRUE)
covered = abs(sim_log_or - log_or_matrix) < critical_value * sim_se
sim_summary = data.frame(
  year = rownames(years),
  bias = colMeans(sim_log_or) - log_or_used,
  sd_estimates = apply(sim_log_or, 2, sd),
  mean_se = colMeans(sim_se),
  coverage = colMeans(covered)
)
show_table(sim_summary, digits = 3)
```

`r if (n_failed == 0) "Every fit converged." else paste(n_failed, "fits did not converge.")`
The biases are small compared with the standard errors (largest absolute bias
`r formatC(max(abs(sim_summary$bias)), format = "f", digits = 3)`, against standard errors of
`r f2(min(sim_summary$mean_se))` to `r f2(max(sim_summary$mean_se))`). The standard errors,
however, are on average
`r round(100 * (1 - mean(sim_summary$mean_se / sim_summary$sd_estimates)))`% smaller than
the standard deviations of the estimates, and the coverages lie between
`r f1(100 * min(sim_summary$coverage))`% and `r f1(100 * max(sim_summary$coverage))`%,
`r if (max(sim_summary$coverage) < 0.925) "all below" else "partly below"` the range of
about 92.5% to 97.5% that 300 samples give for a coverage of 95%. The Wald intervals of the
height of the cline are somewhat too narrow: a nominal 95% interval covers about 90%.

The standard deviation among samples used to simulate, and the mean and median of its
estimates:

```{r}
sd_sample_check = c(simulated = exp(ends_fit$par[["log_sd_group"]]),
                    mean = mean(sim_sd_sample), median = median(sim_sd_sample))
sd_sample_check
```

The estimates of the standard deviation among samples are on average
`r round(100 * abs(1 - sd_sample_check[["mean"]] / sd_sample_check[["simulated"]]))`%
`r if (sd_sample_check[["mean"]] < sd_sample_check[["simulated"]]) "too small" else "too large"`
(`r f2(sd_sample_check[["mean"]])` against `r f2(sd_sample_check[["simulated"]])`). This is
the bias of the maximum likelihood estimate of a variance (Chapter 7, REML): the 70
samples are 70 groups, but the cline uses 12 fixed effects, and each sample has one count,
so the deviations of the samples are estimated from the same counts as the cline. A
standard deviation that is too small makes the standard errors of the cline too small,
which explains part of the low coverage. A REML fit integrates out the fixed effects as
well:

```{r}
reml_obj = MakeADFun(cmb(cline_nll, ends_data), ends_start,
                     random = c("u", "beta_coast", "beta_inland", "beta_steepness",
                                "beta_centre"),
                     silent = TRUE)
reml_fit = optim(par = reml_obj$par, fn = reml_obj$fn, gr = reml_obj$gr,
                 method = "BFGS")
reml_fit$convergence
sd_sample_reml = exp(reml_fit$par[["log_sd_group"]])
sd_sample_reml
```

The REML estimate is `r f2(sd_sample_reml)` against `r f2(sd_sample_check[["simulated"]])`
by maximum likelihood: larger, in the direction and of roughly the size that the
simulation suggests.

::: {.callout-warning title="Pitfall: Wald intervals that are slightly too narrow"}
Under the model itself, the Wald intervals of the odds ratios cover about 90% instead of
95%, partly because the standard deviation among samples is underestimated. The intervals
of @sec-answer should be read as somewhat optimistic. The conclusions do not change: the
1980 and 2004 intervals of the odds ratio are far apart.
:::

# Summary: alternatives, pitfalls and teaching notes {#sec-summary}

**Answer.** Along the east–west transect, the typical frequency of melanics 60 km from the
coast fell from `r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 1)` in 1980 to
`r answer_pct(ends_answer, "far", 5)` in 2004, while 10 km from the coast it stayed at
about `r pct(mean(ends_answer$near_estimate))`%. The odds ratio between the two, the
height of the cline, fell from `r answer_or(ends_answer, 1)` to
`r answer_or(ends_answer, 5)`. The centre (`r f1(centre_ends)` km) and the width
(`r round(4 / steepness_ends)` km) did not change detectably. On the north–south transect
the cline also became shallower between 1980 and 1991, but mainly because melanics
increased near Delft.

**Pitfalls.**

1. The 1980 survey pools 1978 to 1981 and has samples of up to 15,217 beetles; a Binomial
   model without variation among samples gives them nearly all the weight and standard
   errors that are far too small (@sec-design, @sec-choices).
2. The information comes from `r nrow(ew)` samples, not `r big(sum(ew$n))` beetles; the
   heterogeneity chi-square grows with the sample size for the same variation on the
   logit scale (@sec-variation), and DHARMa's dispersion statistic is dominated by the two
   largest samples (@sec-residuals).
3. Different localities were sampled in different surveys (six missing in 2004, after the
   invasion of the harlequin ladybird), so raw means per survey are not comparable
   (@sec-design).
4. A logistic regression with distance as a linear predictor (a GLMM) cannot describe the
   two plateaus (@sec-linear).
5. The random effect per site, the obvious grouping, collapses to zero; the variation is
   among samples (@sec-choices, @sec-two-re). An estimate at the boundary with a converged
   fit is Chapter 8 material.
6. The centre and steepness of a flat cline are not identifiable; they must be shared
   across surveys (@sec-candidates).
7. The typical frequency of the mixed model ($u_j = 0$) is that of the median sample; the
   Beta-Binomial mean $p$ is the mean sample. The difference is small here
   ($\sigma_{\mathrm{sample}} =$ `r f2(sd_sample_ci[1])`).
8. The distances of the two transects have different origins (coast and Delft), the 1980
   Willemstad sample is in both, and the year of the second north–south survey is 1991 in
   the spreadsheet and 1992 in the paper (@sec-ns).
9. The spreadsheet lacks three samples of Table 1 of the 2011 paper; `adalia.csv`
   contains them (`README.md`; they do not change the answer, @sec-sensitivity).
10. The data show a change over time, not its cause; the climate is not in the data
    (@sec-trend).
11. Middelharnis in 1980 (9% of 8,256 beetles) lies below the coastal plateau; a cline
    cannot dip, and only the variation among samples accommodates it.
12. The maximum likelihood estimate of the standard deviation among samples is about
    `r round(100 * abs(1 - sd_sample_check[["mean"]] / sd_sample_check[["simulated"]]))`%
    too small, and the Wald intervals of the odds ratios cover about 90% instead of 95%
    (@sec-simulation).

**Alternatives.**

- The Beta-Binomial distribution instead of the random effect per sample (better by
  `r f1(aic_choice[["Binomial sample"]] - aic_choice[["BetaBinomial none"]])` AIC units,
  same answer; @sec-choices, @sec-sensitivity).
- A REML estimate of the standard deviation among samples (@sec-simulation).
- The trend model with one rate of change of the inland plateau (@sec-trend).
- The candidate `inland` (best by AIC among the survey-factor models), if the question is
  only about the inland frequency.
- Other answer quantities inside the data: the plateaus themselves (close to the
  frequencies at 10 and 60 km here), or the difference between surveys at 60 km (one more
  line of `ADREPORT()`).
- One model for both transects (@sec-ns).
- Both random effects (@sec-two-re; beyond Chapter 7).

**Teaching notes (possible questions for students).**

- Read starting values for the cline from @fig-transect, and derive the width $4/b$ from
  the slope at the centre.
- Calculate the heterogeneity statistic and the standard deviation on the logit scale per
  survey, and explain why one grows with the sample size and the other does not.
- Compare a random effect per site with one per sample, and explain what each assumes
  about the localities.
- Compare the cline with a linear predictor of the logit, and explain why the parameters
  of the cline answer the question better.
- Compare candidates for the change over time and explain why the answer uses `ends`
  although `inland` has a lower AIC.
- Report the frequencies at 10 and 60 km with intervals, and discuss what the data can and
  cannot say about the cause of the change.
